late-delivery.title: A late feed is reported and the rest still loads
late-delivery.promise: When a feed does not arrive, the team is told, and every other report still loads on time.

related.why: When a feed is not just late but broken, an operator can leave it out of the nightly load.

problem.headline: The carrier goes silent and nobody notices for two days
problem.story:
Every evening the carrier sends the day's parcel scans. One day the scans stop coming. No error appears,
because nothing was sent that could go wrong. The nightly load keeps showing the same old numbers. Two days
later a manager notices that no scan has arrived for two days, and everyone asks how long this has been going on.
problem.cost: Customer service promises delivery dates from numbers that are two days old.

visual.caption: A silent feed looks exactly like a quiet day.

idea.headline: Each night we check when every feed last arrived
points: Every [[feed]] has an agreed deadline, here one day.
After the [[nightly load]], a separate check compares the newest arrival of each feed with its deadline.
The check only reports, so the feeds that did arrive are still loaded.

visual.caption: Late is a conversation with the sender, not a reason to stop everything.

skip-one-table.promise: When one feed arrives broken, an operator skips it for tonight and every other report is still on time.

related.why: The skip list is another setting an operator can change in a minute, without a new release.

problem.headline: One broken carrier file leaves management with yesterday's numbers
problem.story:
At 02:00 the carrier sends a file in which 3 scans have no scan number. The automatic checks stop the work for
everything that depends on the carrier, and the night ends in red. The management report, which combines orders
and deliveries, is not refreshed. At 08:00 management opens it and reads yesterday's numbers. The carrier team
needs a day to fix its file.
problem.cost: Management works from a report that is a day old, because of 3 bad scans from one carrier.

visual.caption: Everything that depends on the carrier stops until the carrier is fixed.

strict-where-it-matters.title: Messy test data is fine in development, never in production
strict-where-it-matters.promise: The same check only warns while we try things out, and stops the load where real customers depend on it.

problem.headline: Either testers are blocked, or bad data reaches production
problem.story:
Testers fill the practice copy of the shop with made-up orders, and some have invalid customer numbers. If the
check on customer numbers is strict everywhere, every practice night stops and nobody can try anything. If it
is relaxed everywhere, an invalid customer number can reach the real shop one day, and finance invoices a
customer who does not exist.
problem.cost: Testers lose days to stopped nights, or finance sends an invoice to a customer who does not exist.

left.title: Strict everywhere
items: Practice orders stop every practice night.

right.title: Relaxed everywhere
items: An invalid customer number reaches the real shop.
Finance finds out at invoice time.

switchover-date.title: Switching to a new scan format on an agreed day
switchover-date.promise: The carrier changes its scan format on one day, and we switch on that day, so no parcel scan goes missing.

related.why: The switch day is a setting an operator can change without a new release, like the skip list in that scenario.

problem.headline: Parcel scans in the carrier's new format vanish from the report
problem.story:
The carrier sends one scan for every step of a parcel's journey. Four days ago it started using a new scan
format. Our report only understands the old one. Nothing crashes and no alarm rings: the new scans arrive, but
the report cannot read them. Parcels that were delivered look as if they never left the warehouse, and it
stays that way every day until someone changes the report.
problem.cost: Customer service cannot see five days of parcel scans, about 110 a day, and tells customers their parcel is lost.

visual.caption: From the day of the change, every scan arrives and none can be read.

idea.headline: Read old scans the old way and new scans the new way
points: We keep two readers side by side: one for the old scan format and one for the new one.
Every scan goes to exactly one reader, chosen by the day it arrived, so none is lost or counted twice.
The switch day is a [[setting]]: an [[operator]] changes it in a minute, with no new [[release]].

checked-before-merge.title: Every change is rehearsed in a sandbox before it is accepted
checked-before-merge.promise: A mistake in a proposed change is caught by an automatic rehearsal, long before any report is wrong.

problem.headline: One small change makes every order count three times
problem.story:
A developer improves the orders table and, by mistake, every order now appears three times. The change looks
tiny, so nobody checks it. On Monday the management report says the shop took three times as many orders as it
really did. Finance has already sent that number to the board.
problem.cost: Finance sends the board an order count three times too high, and the developers lose a day finding the cause.

visual.caption: One wrong step and everything after it is wrong too.

idea.headline: Every proposed change is rehearsed first, and a failed rehearsal blocks it
points: The automatic check rebuilds only what the change touches, plus the reports that depend on it.
It does this in a [[sandbox]], a private corner of the database named after the change, and runs every [[test]] there.
A red result blocks the change, and the sandbox is thrown away afterwards, whatever the result.

visual.caption: The mistake is found by the rehearsal, not by the people who read the report.

lines.note: The sandbox is named after the proposed change, so two rehearsals never disturb each other.
The change is tried on top of everybody else's latest work.
Only the changed reports and those that depend on them are rebuilt and checked.

house-rules.title: Sloppy or risky code is refused before it is saved
house-rules.promise: A robot tidies every change and refuses known bad habits, so reviewers can focus on the content.

problem.headline: One banned habit slips through reviews and blanks a report
problem.story:
Every developer writes code in their own layout. Reviewers spend their time arguing about spaces and capital
letters, and miss the real problem: one developer used a date function that formats the month differently on
the new system. The monthly report shows blank months, and nobody notices until finance asks why October is
missing.
problem.cost: Finance works from a monthly report with blank months, and reviewers lose hours on layout instead of content.

visual.caption: The slip is old and well known, but nothing stops it.

idea.headline: A robot checks every change at the moment it is saved
points: It rewrites the code into one standard layout, so everybody's work looks the same.
It refuses code that uses a habit on the team's banned list, and says which rule was broken.
Reviewers see only tidy code that follows the rules, and spend their time on what the code means.

Dana and Sam are both improving the customers table. Dana builds her version and spends an hour checking the
numbers. Meanwhile Sam builds his version into the same place. Dana's table is replaced under her hands, and her
hour of checking was about a table that no longer exists. Nobody knows which version is the right one.
problem.cost: Dana loses an hour of checking, and every report that reads the shared table shows whatever was built last.

back-in-seconds.title: A bad release is undone in seconds
back-in-seconds.promise: Going back to yesterday's version is changing one number, not repairing anything.

related.why: This is where the numbered versions are explained. Here a second version is made for you while the demo gets ready.

problem.headline: A bad release at 8:00 shows wrong totals until 14:00
problem.story:
A new release goes live at 8:00. At 9:00 the sales team sees wrong totals. The developers cannot simply put
yesterday's state back, because nobody has it in one piece. They repair the new code under pressure, and the
wrong totals stay on screen all morning.
problem.cost: Sales works with wrong figures for 5 hours, and the rushed repair risks new mistakes.

visual.caption: Five hours of wrong totals for a problem that one setting could have undone in seconds.

idea.headline: Going back means telling the environment to run the previous number
points: Every version is kept as a sealed package, so yesterday's version still exists exactly as it was.
Going back is changing one setting: the number the environment must run.
The cause can then be found without pressure, and the repaired version goes live again as a new number.

visual.caption: First make it right again. Then find out what went wrong.

code.title: The environment runs whichever number it is told

With no number set, nothing runs. There is never a guess.

lines.text: f"Airflow Variable '{DBT_IMAGE_TAG_VARIABLE}' is not set: no dbt image was deployed to '{ENV}' yet. "
f"Run the deploy job for a tag (it runs: airflow variables set {DBT_IMAGE_TAG_VARIABLE} <tag>)."

lines.note: The sealed package with that number is the one used. Old ones are still there.

no-secret-fixes.title: A fix made by hand in production is detected
no-secret-fixes.promise: Before every release the stack compares the real database with the code and stops on hand-made changes.

problem.headline: A fix made by hand at night vanishes in the next release
problem.story:
On a Friday night a customer table in production is missing a column that support needs. An engineer adds it
by hand, directly in the live database, and goes to bed. Nobody writes it down. Three weeks later a normal
release rebuilds the table from the code, and the column silently disappears.
problem.cost: Support loses a column they relied on for 3 weeks, and nobody can say why it stopped working.

visual.caption: The fix worked for 3 weeks, but only the engineer knew about it.

idea.headline: Before every release the stack compares the real database with the code
points: The first thing a release does is look for any [[hand-made change]] in the real database.
If it finds one, it stops before anything is built and names the table, the person and the time.
The change must first be put into the code, where it is recorded and reviewed. Then the release continues.

visual.caption: The release refuses to run over something it does not know about.

numbered-versions.title: Every environment runs one exact, numbered version
numbered-versions.promise: The question 'which version is running in production?' always has one exact answer.

problem.headline: Nobody can say which version of the code runs in production
problem.story:
On Tuesday the sales report shows odd figures. Support asks the developers: which version of the code produced
this? One developer thinks it is last week's, another thinks Monday's fix is already in. Three people spend the
morning comparing files by hand before they can even start looking for the cause.
problem.cost: Every problem takes hours longer to solve: three people spend a whole morning comparing files.

visual.caption: The search for the version costs more than the search for the cause.

idea.headline: Every accepted change gets a number, and each environment runs one number
points: Accepting a change gives it the next version number automatically, such as v1.0.1.
That number is turned into a sealed package of the code, and a sealed package never changes.
Each [[environment]] is told which number to run, so one glance answers the question.

visual.caption: Like the edition number printed in a book.

code.title: A new number is chosen after every accepted change

lines.note: Find the highest number used so far.
A new feature moves the middle number up, for example v1.1.0.
A small fix moves the last number up, for example v1.0.1.

code.file_label: The instructions for numbering a version

code.title: The number becomes a sealed package

lines.note: This tool packs the code into one sealed package.
The package carries the number, and nobody edits it afterwards.

code.file_label: The instructions for packing a version

code.title: Each environment looks up the number it must run

lines.text: """dbt-vdp:<Variable dbt_image_tag>. The tag is set by the deploy job; unset means nothing was deployed yet."""

lines.note: Each environment keeps one setting with its version number.
If no number was set, nothing runs. There is never a guess.

lines.text: f"Airflow Variable '{DBT_IMAGE_TAG_VARIABLE}' is not set: no dbt image was deployed to '{ENV}' yet. "
f"Run the deploy job for a tag (it runs: airflow variables set {DBT_IMAGE_TAG_VARIABLE} <tag>)."

lines.note: The package with exactly that number is the one that runs.

one-team-not-ready.title: Take one team's change out of a release
one-team-not-ready.promise: When one team is not ready, only that team's change waits and the other team ships.

related.why: Each finished change gets a version number. The unfinished one is taken out by its number.

problem.headline: One team's unfinished change holds back another team's finished one
problem.story:
Two teams have finished their work and both changes sit in the next release, planned for tomorrow. Late today the
reviews team finds that their figures are not yet right. The payments team is fine. Without a way to take out one
change, the choice is to delay everybody or to ship something unfinished.
problem.cost: Finance waits a whole release cycle for a payments overview that was ready, or marketing gets review numbers nobody trusts.

visual.caption: Two changes, one release, one deadline.

idea.headline: One team's change can be taken out, and the rest ships
points: The release gets its own line of work, separate from the daily work, so the daily work never stops.
An unfinished change is taken out of the release only, by its version number, and stays in the daily work.
The release is checked again as a whole and goes live under its own number. The team that waited joins the next one.

visual.caption: A release is a list of changes, and one item can be crossed off.

code.title: The whole release is checked again after the change is taken out

lines.note: A release is checked completely, not only the changed parts.
Any line of work named release/<year>-<quarter> gets this check automatically.

code.file_label: The instructions for the automatic checks

code.title: Going live gives the release its own number

lines.note: The release name, for example 2026-Q4, is read from the message of the final step.

lines.text: latest_rel=$(git tag -l | grep -E '^[0-9]{4}-Q[1-4]\.' | sort -V | tail -n 1 | awk -F. '{print $1}')

lines.note: It looks for earlier numbers of the same release.
The first time, the release is numbered .0. Later fixes count up.

code.file_label: The instructions for numbering a release

right-keys-only.title: The robot that builds development cannot touch production
right-keys-only.promise: Each environment has its own robot with keys to its own rooms only, so a mix-up cannot damage production.

problem.headline: A testing robot pointed at production empties the real customer list
problem.story:
The program that builds the test copy of the system has one set of keys that open every door. One afternoon its
settings are copied from a test setup to the real one by mistake. At night it does what it is told, in the wrong
place: the real customers table is rebuilt from test data, and customer service sees an empty list.
problem.cost: Customer service cannot look anyone up until the real table is restored, and customers notice.

nodes.label: Test settings
nodes.note: Copied to the real system by mistake

visual.caption: One wrong setting is enough, when the keys open everything.

idea.headline: Every robot's keys open only its own environment
points: Development, validation and production each have their own [[robot account]], and the development robot has no key for production.
People get their own keys too: they can work in development and only look in validation and production.
A mistake becomes a refusal with a clear message, instead of damage.

visual.caption: The safety does not depend on anyone remembering to be careful.

code.title: What each environment's robot may do

lines.note: This block is applied separately to each environment, so each robot only gets its own rights.

GRANT SELECT, SHOW VIEW ON __ENV___landing.* TO ROLE '__ENV___dbt';
lines.note: The robot may only read the incoming data. It builds the reports.

GRANT SELECT, SHOW VIEW ON __ENV___edw_dv_rdv.* TO ROLE '__ENV___reader';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON __ENV___edw_dv_rdv.* TO ROLE '__ENV___dbt';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON __ENV___edw_dv_bdv.* TO ROLE '__ENV___admin';

every-run-on-record.title: Every run and every check is written down
every-run-on-record.promise: The question "what ran last night, how long did it take, what failed" always has an answer, in plain tables.

related.why: The mail reports tonight's failure; the record keeps the history of every night.

problem.headline: Nobody can say what ran last night or how long it took
problem.story:
One morning the management report is late. The manager asks: did the night run? How long did it take? Did a
check fail? Nobody knows. The answers are in the [[log]], which is thrown away after a few days, so the team can
only guess. A table that gets a little slower every week goes unnoticed until the night no longer finishes
before morning.
problem.cost: The team has to search for every answer about last night, and slow tables are found only when the morning report is late.

nodes.label: The log
nodes.note: Thrown away after a few days

visual.caption: Without a record, the past is gone.

idea.headline: Every step and every check is written down when the night ends
points: At the end of each night, every step and check is added to one table: its name, result, time and rows.
The table sits next to the data, so anyone allowed to read the reports can ask it questions.
Two ready-made lists are built on it: today's failed checks and the slowest tables.

nodes.label: The night ends
nodes.note: Every step and check has a result

nodes.label: One row per step and check

visual.caption: The record turns "I think so" into a number.

code.title: The end of every run triggers the writing

lines.note: As soon as a run is over, whatever happened is written down.

lines.text: - "{% if env_var('LOG_RUN_RESULTS', '') == 'TRUE' and target.name == 'run'%}{{ log_dbt_results(results) }}{% endif %}"
lines.note: Only the real nightly runs are written down, not experiments.

How long it took.

one-clear-mail.title: A failed night produces one clear mail
one-clear-mail.promise: When the nightly load fails, the team gets one short mail that says what failed, not a wall of text.

related.why: After reading the mail and fixing the cause, only the failed part is run again.

problem.headline: The night fails, and the cause is buried in hundreds of lines
problem.story:
At 03:10 the nightly load stops. In the morning the person on duty opens the [[log]]: hundreds of lines from a
dozen steps, with the one line that matters somewhere in the middle. Twenty minutes later it is clear that three
orders have no order number. By then the reports have been wrong for hours, and colleagues are asking in the
chat what happened.
problem.cost: Every failure costs the person on duty about 20 minutes of reading before anyone can start fixing.

visual.caption: Nothing tells the team where to look.

idea.headline: One mail per failed night, with the answer at the top
points: When any step fails, one last step collects what went wrong and writes it up.
The mail names the failed check and counts what succeeded, failed and was skipped.
It is sent once per night, however many steps failed, with the last 40 log lines below it.

visual.caption: The mail does the reading so the team can do the fixing.

code.title: A last step that runs only after a failure

lines.note: On a good night this step stays idle; any failed step starts it.

lines.text: """One mail: dbt findings of the failed task(s), run_results.json, the last log lines."""
lines.note: It sends exactly one mail: the findings, the check results and the last log lines.

lines.note: One mail per night, whichever step failed.
Every step of the night leads to the mail step, so any failure sends it.

rebuild-without-downtime.title: Rebuilding a big table while people keep reading it
rebuild-without-downtime.promise: A big table is rebuilt next to the old one and swapped in at once, so readers never see an empty table.

problem.headline: During the rebuild, finance sees an empty table, then a half-filled one
problem.story:
The invoice table holds 100,000 rows and must be rebuilt after a correction. The usual way is to empty it and
fill it again, and that takes ninety minutes. During those ninety minutes finance opens the report and sees 0
rows, then 33,000, then 66,000. Someone sends a half-filled total to the bank. The correct number appears only
when the rebuild is finished.
problem.cost: Finance works with a wrong total for ninety minutes, and nobody can tell how wrong it is.

visual.caption: For ninety minutes nobody can trust the rows they see.

idea.headline: Fill a new copy beside the old table, then swap it in
points: The old table stays untouched and readable the whole time.
The new copy is filled part by part; if one part fails, only that part is repeated, in smaller pieces.
The new copy is checked first, and only then swapped for the old table, so readers notice nothing.

nodes.label: The swap
nodes.note: The new copy takes the old name

visual.caption: Until the swap, everything readers see is the old, complete table.

code.title: Each big table says how it can be cut into parts

lines.note: Every row has its own key, and the parts are cut on that key.
The table says it can be cut into equal parts, loaded one by one.

code.file_label: The recipe for the practice table

code.title: The swap is the only moment readers are affected

lines.note: The old table is moved aside as a backup, not deleted.

lines.text: {% do run_query("alter table " ~ names.new ~ " rename to " ~ names.orig) %}
lines.note: The new copy takes over the old name.

redo-only-what-failed.title: After a fix, only the failed part runs again
redo-only-what-failed.promise: When a night fails and the cause is fixed, the retry redoes only what failed and what waits for it.

related.why: The mail tells the team what failed, so they know what to fix before they retry.

problem.headline: Fixing three bad orders costs a whole second night of work
problem.story:
The nightly load builds 28 tables. At 03:10 it stops because three orders have no order number. The cause is
fixed in ten minutes, but the only way forward is to start the whole night again from the beginning. All 28
tables are rebuilt, including the ones that were fine, and the management report is late for the morning
meeting.
problem.cost: Management waits for all 28 tables to be rebuilt after a ten-minute fix, and the morning meeting runs on old numbers.

visual.caption: Everything is redone, even what was fine.

idea.headline: A retry remembers what worked and redoes only the rest
points: After every run, the result of every step is saved: what worked, what failed and what was skipped.
A retry reads that saved result and redoes only the failed step and whatever waits for it.
A brand-new night starts from the top, so a retry cannot mix in results from an old night.

nodes.label: Redone
nodes.note: The failed part and what waits for it

visual.caption: The saved result of the first attempt is what makes the short retry possible.

code.title: The second attempt knows it is a retry

lines.note: From the second attempt on, the night knows it is a retry.

lines.text: f"RETRY MODE (attempt {ti.try_number}): This task will execute 'dbt retry' "

lines.note: It looks for the saved results of the first attempt.

code.file_label: The list of steps of the nightly load

code.title: A retry becomes a different command

lines.note: Instead of building everything, the command retries only what did not succeed.
It reads the saved results from where the first attempt left them.
